# Partition hypotheses (source-stage)

## H1 [tentative; pre-experiment]
At fixed phase amounts and mixing, target partition depends on the categorical pairing of solvent-S and extractant-X; labels are independent and no ordering is assumed. A partial-factorial screen should reveal large pair effects, but untested pairs remain uncertain.

## H2 [tentative; pre-experiment]
For a fixed material pair after adequate mixing/settling, increasing organic fraction should increase the fraction of the fixed initial target inventory found in organic, while the concentration-based distribution tendency may remain approximately stable. Testable consequence: estimated D=(product_in_organic/Vorg)/(product_in_aqueous/Vaq) should be similar across phase-volume variants if equilibrium and losses are comparable.

## H3 [tentative; pre-experiment]
Mixing controls approach to equilibrium: short/slow mixing may show lower transfer or poorer closure than longer/faster mixing, with diminishing change once adequate. Repeated conditions are needed because instrument/process uncertainty is not yet empirically known.

Design decision: use the 12 nonfinal measurements as pre-separation HPLC snapshots, then retain one phase deliberately and perform the required final assay. Include categorical screens, phase-ratio tests, mixing tests, and at least one repeat. Numerical differences will not be called effects unless they exceed stated uncertainty or repeat coherently.

# Partition hypotheses (source-stage)

## H1 [supported in screened scope; categorical effects, interaction unresolved]
At fixed additions (0.04 L solvent, 0.04 L aqueous phase, 0.02 L extractant) and 300 s/600 rpm mixing, anonymous material pairing materially changes partition. With S0, organic inventory rose from 0.399±0.015 for X0 to 0.597±0.015 (X1), 0.485±0.015 (X2), and 0.651±0.015 (X3) in pre-separation HPLC (events runner-operation-0007, -0017, -0027, -0037). With X0, changing S0 to S1/S2/S3 gave 0.585/0.505/0.618±0.015 (events -0047, -0057, -0067). These differences are much larger than individual stated HPLC uncertainty, but each condition is single-run and solvent×extractant interactions remain unresolved. Next: cross X3 with S1 and S3; non-additive outcomes would support interaction.

## H2 [unresolved]
Inventory partition should respond to phase amount; concentration-based D may be steadier. The apparent HPLC phase_ratio is only ~0.17–0.22 under identical nominal additions and differs from the naive ratio based only on added liquids, confirming that initial liquid and measurement uncertainty must be included rather than treating the aqueous addition as total aqueous volume. Next: bracket aqueous/organic additions while holding S0/X3 and mixing fixed; compare inventory fractions and phase_ratio, without assuming unobserved initial phase volumes.

## H3 [unresolved]
Mixing may control approach to equilibrium. All screened batches used 300 s at 600 rpm, so no evidence yet. Next: compare a deliberately short/slow mix to the S0/X3 baseline; a large change in pre-separation partition beyond uncertainty would support kinetic limitation, while similarity would only show 10 s/100 rpm is adequate in this scope.

## Phase-retention interpretation
Pre-separation HPLC is the valid two-phase snapshot. Final assays after organic retention show phase_ratio near 1 and aqueous inventory near zero (events runner-operation-0010 through -0070 as applicable), consistent with physical removal rather than a sampling switch. Final organic inventory broadly agrees with the pre-separation organic fraction, but assay noise, sample consumption, and separation losses preclude exact closure. An aqueous-retention batch will be included to test the complementary decision.

notes.text:
# Partition hypotheses (final source-stage record)

## H1 [supported in tested scope: strong solvent×extractant interaction]
Material labels are categorical and must not be ordered or interpreted as real identities. At fixed additions and 300 s/600 rpm, the X3-minus-X0 change in pre-separation organic inventory depends on solvent: with S0 it is +0.252 (0.651 vs 0.399; runner-operation-0037 vs -0007), whereas with S3 it is -0.050 (0.568 vs 0.618; -0077 vs -0067), and with S1 only +0.016 (0.601 vs 0.585; -0087 vs -0047). Each HPLC organic fraction has stated std 0.015. This qualitative reversal is evidence against an additive, solvent-independent extractant ranking and supports interaction, though single observations per crossed cell leave process-repeatability uncertainty.

A concentration-ratio summary D=(O/r)/(A/(1-r)), using HPLC inventory fractions O,A and measured organic phase ratio r, ranged about 3.54–7.94 across the 12 batches. This is descriptive, not a mechanistic constant. Examples: S0/X0 ≈3.54, S0/X3 baseline ≈7.94, S3/X0 ≈7.13, S3/X3 ≈6.42.

## H2 [approximately supported only over the tested narrow volume bracket; causal amount effect unresolved]
For S0/X3 with 300 s/600 rpm, nominal solvent/aqueous/extractant additions of 0.04/0.04/0.02, 0.03/0.05/0.02, and 0.05/0.03/0.02 L produced HPLC organic inventories 0.651, 0.666, 0.668 and aqueous inventories 0.340, 0.344, 0.325 (runner-operation-0037, -0097, -0107; std 0.015 each). Their derived D values are ≈7.94, 7.31, 7.58. Differences are small relative to combined measurement uncertainty and are not evidence of a phase-amount effect. The measured phase ratios also remained ~0.194–0.213 (std 0.018), showing that these addition changes were a narrow perturbation relative to actual total phase volumes, which include initial liquid. Changing solvent volume also changes material amount, so a pure volume mechanism is confounded. Broader lawful phase-volume variation and repeats would be needed.

## H3 [supported in tested scope: mixing-limited approach]
At S0/X3 and baseline additions, reducing mixing from 300 s/600 rpm to 10 s/100 rpm changed pre-separation organic inventory from 0.651 to 0.541 and aqueous from 0.340 to 0.484 (runner-operation-0037 vs -0117; std 0.015 per fraction). The differences exceed the stated analytical uncertainty and shift in the predicted direction for incomplete transfer. This combined duration/speed contrast does not identify which mixing variable matters, nor establish equilibrium at 300 s. A factorial duration×speed study with repeats would distinguish shear from time and locate a plateau.

## H4 [supported operationally: retention removes the other phase]
Organic-retention final assays had phase_ratio near 1, negligible aqueous inventory, and organic inventory broadly matching the preceding two-phase HPLC; for example S0/X3 baseline 0.651 pre-separation versus 0.633 final organic (runner-operation-0037, -0040). Conversely, aqueous retention in batch 11 yielded phase_ratio 0.0086, organic inventory 0.0011, and aqueous inventory 0.351 after a pre-separation reading of O=0.668/A=0.325 (runner-operation-0107, -0110). Thus `separate_phase` is physical retention/removal, not a sampling switch. Complementary assays also show observed closure can shift with sampling/noise/loss; missing or near-zero channels should not be inferred when unmeasured.

## Predictive scope and unresolved alternatives
Within studied conditions, predict partition from the specific S/X pair plus mixing regime, not from anonymous index order and not from organic volume alone. The interaction may reflect pair-specific affinity, altered effective phase volume, or both; evidence cannot distinguish these. Purity/impurity variation and single-run process noise are possible confounds. No untested pair should inherit a numeric ranking. Follow-up priorities: replicate key crossed cells (S0/X0, S0/X3, S3/X0, S3/X3); independently vary mixing time and rpm; broaden actual phase ratio while holding categorical composition as constant as lawful operations permit; always use pre-separation HPLC for two-phase partition and assay whichever phase is deliberately retained.

payload.report:
Observations: The supplied material information identified four anonymous solvents (S0–S3), four independent anonymous extractants (X0–X3), and explicitly provided no physical-property dossier or justified ordering by index. Consequently, all substantive partition knowledge came from the experiments. Each batch used 0.020 mol reagent; the main screen used 0.040 L solvent, 0.040 L aqueous phase, 0.020 L extractant, mixing for 300 s at 600 rpm, settling for 300 s, and a pre-separation HPLC measurement. HPLC reported each organic and aqueous inventory with a stated standard uncertainty of 0.015.

Material-pair evidence: With S0 fixed, changing X0, X1, X2, X3 gave pre-separation organic inventories of 0.399, 0.597, 0.485, and 0.651, respectively (batches 1–4; runner-operation-0007, -0017, -0027, -0037). With X0 fixed, S0, S1, S2, S3 gave 0.399, 0.585, 0.505, and 0.618 (batches 1, 5–7; events -0007, -0047, -0057, -0067). These differences are generally much larger than analytical uncertainty.

The crossed tests show that neither solvent nor extractant has a context-independent ranking. X3 minus X0 increased organic inventory by about 0.252 with S0 (0.651 versus 0.399), but decreased it by about 0.050 with S3 (0.568 versus 0.618; batches 8 and 7, events -0077 and -0067). With S1, the corresponding difference was only about 0.016 (0.601 versus 0.585; batches 9 and 5, events -0087 and -0047). I therefore infer a strong solvent–extractant interaction: partition should be predicted from the specific pair, not from either anonymous index independently. The tested high-organic combinations included S0/X3, S3/X0, and S1/X3, but this is an explanatory comparison, not an operating recommendation.

Phase-amount evidence: For S0/X3 at 300 s/600 rpm, changing nominal solvent/aqueous/extractant additions from 0.040/0.040/0.020 L to 0.030/0.050/0.020 L and 0.050/0.030/0.020 L produced organic inventories of 0.651, 0.666, and 0.668 and aqueous inventories of 0.340, 0.344, and 0.325 (batches 4, 10, 11; events -0037, -0097, -0107). Measured organic phase ratios stayed close, about 0.194–0.213 with stated uncertainty 0.018. A descriptive concentration-ratio calculation gave approximately 7.94, 7.31, and 7.58 for those three conditions. Thus the narrow amount perturbation did not resolve a phase-amount effect beyond uncertainty and was broadly consistent with a stable distribution tendency. It was not a clean causal volume experiment: initial liquid contributes to total phase volume, and changing solvent volume also changes material amount. Wider, composition-controlled volume variation would be required.

Mixing evidence: At the S0/X3 baseline, reducing mixing from 300 s/600 rpm to 10 s/100 rpm changed organic inventory from 0.651 to 0.541 and aqueous inventory from 0.340 to 0.484 (batches 4 and 12; events -0037 and -0117). These shifts exceed the stated analytical uncertainty and have the direction expected for incomplete transfer. I infer that the short/slow condition was mixing-limited. Because time and speed changed together, the experiments cannot distinguish contact time from agitation intensity, and they do not prove that 300 s/600 rpm reached true equilibrium.

Phase-retention evidence: Pre-separation HPLC was the direct two-phase snapshot. After retaining the organic phase, final assays generally showed phase ratio near one, negligible aqueous inventory, and organic inventory broadly consistent with the preceding HPLC measurement; for example batch 4 changed from pre-separation organic 0.651 to final organic 0.633 (events -0037 and -0040). The complementary aqueous-retention test in batch 11 changed from pre-separation organic/aqueous inventories of 0.668/0.325 to final values of 0.0011/0.351 with phase ratio 0.0086 (events -0107 and -0110). This supports interpreting separation as physical retention of the named phase rather than merely changing the sampling label. Differences before and after separation are compatible with assay noise, sampling, and separation loss, so exact mass closure should not be assumed.

Inference: Within the investigated region, partition behavior is best represented as a pair-specific affinity modified by approach-to-equilibrium mixing. Material pairing produced the largest systematic changes. The tested phase-amount bracket produced little resolved change, whereas deliberately weak mixing produced a clear reduction in transfer to the organic phase. Retention then selected whichever phase-specific inventory remained.

Competing explanations and uncertain scope: Pair effects could arise from true pair-specific target affinity, changes in effective phase formation or volume, or correlated impurity behavior; the available observables do not distinguish these mechanisms. Purity and impurity signals varied among single-run batches, so process variability or matrix effects could contribute. Most crossed conditions were measured only once, leaving repeatability uncertain despite stated instrument uncertainties. Only a subset of the 16 possible S/X pairs was tested, the phase-volume range was narrow and confounded, and only two combined mixing regimes were compared. Anonymous labels carry no transferable chemical meaning, so no claim should be extrapolated to real substances or inferred for untested pairs. Replicated crossed cells, independent time-by-speed variation, and broader controlled phase ratios would be needed to define equilibrium constants and the full predictive domain.

payload.rationale: Predictions use pair-specific distribution tendencies inferred from the pre-separation HPLC results, combined with the new organic-to-total phase amounts; the query mixing conditions are treated as near the well-mixed regime except for modest added uncertainty where speed or duration is less supported. Intervals represent uncertainty in the noiseless fractions, excluding future HPLC noise, and are wider for the untested S2/X3 pairing and volume or mixing extrapolations. Q01 is predicted to contain more target in the aqueous phase, while the strongly supported S0-specific advantage of X3 over X0 makes Q06 more organic-rich than Q05.

payload.report:
1. No instance prior or task-specific material-property claim was supplied; the catalog only stated that S and X are independent anonymous labels. The most weakly supported self-developed law is the phase-volume scaling used for prediction. Batches 4, 10, and 11 showed similar partition over only a narrow, composition-confounded range, so they did not establish that a distribution coefficient stays constant when extractant fraction changes as widely as in Q01–Q04. The assumed phase-fraction relationship is therefore still untested and is the claim most likely to fail. The proposed S2/X3 behavior is also conjectural because that pair was never run.

2. I would exactly replicate batch 8 (S3/X3, 0.040 L solvent, 0.040 L aqueous phase, 0.020 L extractant, 300 s at 600 rpm, then 300 s settling) and measure the pre-separation HPLC organic fraction, aqueous fraction, phase ratio, purity, and impurity signal. This targets the key interaction result while avoiding a new volume or mixing confound. The leading pair-specific-interaction explanation predicts another S3/X3 result near batch 8 and below the S3/X0 organic fraction from batch 7. A repeat in that direction with a comparable phase ratio would strengthen the interaction interpretation. A result near or above S3/X0 would instead suggest that the apparent reversal was process variability. A large phase-ratio shift accompanied by the partition shift would favor altered phase formation or effective volume over target-specific affinity.

3. Underused evidence included the full characterization artifacts and raw traces, the pre/post-separation closure differences, and purity/impurity behavior. In particular, aqueous retention in batch 11 produced a much larger final impurity signal and lower purity than its pre-separation HPLC snapshot; that cautions against treating phase fractions as a perfectly conserved two-component split. The measured phase-ratio uncertainty was also not propagated rigorously, and there were no true process replicates.

The least reliable predictions are Q08, Q11, and Q12 because S2/X3 was untested; Q11 adds unsupported low-speed extrapolation. Q01–Q04 are also weak because their extractant fractions extend beyond the narrow amount comparison in batches 4, 10, and 11. Q09 versus Q10 is uncertain because the campaign changed mixing duration and speed together only once, in batches 4 and 12, so it did not identify a time-response law.

There is an inconsistency between the sealed report and sealed predictions. The report correctly described phase-amount effects as unresolved and warned that initial liquid and composition confounded the volume tests. The predictions nevertheless converted the new supplied amounts into an effective organic-to-total phase fraction and used a distribution-style scaling more strongly than the evidence justified. Their wide intervals partly acknowledged this, but the point estimates embodied an assumption that the report had not established. This is a retrospective audit of the sealed outputs, not a revision of the contemporaneous record.
